newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti investors nervous before meeting.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti investors nervous before meeting.

text.p: Investors in Italy's troubled hi-tech company Olivetti steeled their nerves ahead of talks by market regulators on Thursday with managers and a former executive who has cast doubt on Olivetti's accounts.
Olivetti shares were suspended on the Milan stock exchange ahead of the meeting in Rome called by bourse regulator Consob.

It was the latest twist in a week of high drama which had seen Olivetti's stock price plunge and then stabilise after tycoon Carlo De Benedetti resigned as chairman on Tuesday, ending 18 years at the helm.

Olivetti's chief executive Francesco Caio, widely seen as having won out in a boardroom power struggle with De Benedetti, has been summoned to Rome by Consob along with De Benedetti's successor as chairman Antonio Tesone and other officials.
They will meet the regulators after separate talks by Consob with Renzo Francesconi, a former Olivetti director-general who resigned on Wednesday after only six weeks at the company.
Francesconi has expressed misgivings about the way the company presented its results for the first half of 1996.
Olivetti said on Thursday that Francesconi's comments were completely unfounded and that it had instructed lawyers "to take action in defence of the company's moral standing."
Olivetti, which has not made a profit since 1990, announced a pre-tax loss for the first six months of 1996 of 440.2 billion lire ($291 million).

Francesconi was quoted in newspapers on Thursday as saying after he announced he was standing down: "You can make compromises over strategic plans but you really can't do that with figures and the accounts."
Milan financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore said in a front page editorial that the implications of Francesconi's remarks were "very serious if they are authentic, irresponsible if false".
Equity analysts who took part in a conference call with Caio on Wednesday evening said he had evaded questions about the presentation of the half-yearly accounts.
"Caio was asked about it but did not say anything," said Angela Dean, European technology analyst at Morgan Stanley. "It's all rather confusing and it does not help build confidence."
An Italian share analyst who listened in on the call expressed alarm at the state of Olivetti's finances.

"I am very worried. I think the company is totally out of control. Caio talked for two hours and said practically nothing," said the analyst with a major Milan finance house who asked not to be identified.
Foreign institutional investors, who now own about 70 percent of Olivetti, have put strong pressure on the company to give more information about where it is heading.

Questions over the true state of the Olivetti were likely to focus on the group's stricken personal computer interests. This has been a huge drain on cash in recent years and many industry observers believe Olivetti should cut its losses and get out of the business altogether before it drags down the entire group.
Olivetti is engaged in a painful transition from PCs, which made fat profits in the 1980s before plunging into the red, to telecommunications, widely seen as the moneymaker of the 1990s.
An investment banker in Milan said it was not clear what value Olivetti was attaching in its balance sheet to unsold stocks of obsolete 386 and 486 series PCs.
"You can write these down at cost price or you can increase their value in the balance sheet by writing them down at the market price," said the Milan banker, who has close knowledge of the company.
If Olivetti has more bad news in store for investors it had nothing to lose by giving it out without delay, said analysts.
Caio, appointed chief executive officer at Olivetti two months ago, was in a position to heap blame for the group's difficulties on its previous management team handpicked by De Benedetti, they said.
